extracted.intended_audience: Guardian News & Media (GNM) journalists, freelancers and external contributors worldwide
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive editorial code and accompanying guidance setting out the professional, ethical and legal standards GNM expects all staff, casual workers and external contributors to follow when producing journalism across print, online and social platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must take care not to publish inaccurate, misleading or distorted information or images, including headlines not supported by the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant inaccuracies, misleading statements or distortions must be corrected promptly and with due prominence and, where appropriate, an apology published. Give a fair opportunity to reply to significant inaccuracies when reasonably called for. Distinguish clearly between comment/conjecture and fact. Report fairly and accurately the outcome of any defamation action involving the publication unless an agreed settlement or statement provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone is entitled to respect for their private and family life, home, health and correspondence, including digital communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must justify intrusions into private life without consent, taking account of the complainant's public disclosures and whether the material is already or will become public. It is unacceptable to photograph individuals without consent in places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy. Clauses marked * may have public interest exceptions; intrusions require senior duty editor authorisation and public interest justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not engage in intimidation, harassment or persistent pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not persist in questioning, telephoning, pursuing or photographing individuals once asked to desist; do not remain on property when asked to leave or follow individuals. If requested, identify yourself as a GNM journalist. Editors must ensure these principles are observed and avoid using non-compliant material from other sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrusion into grief or shock
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases involving personal grief or shock, inquiries and approaches must be made with sympathy and discretion, and publication handled sensitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions should not restrict the right to report on court proceedings, including inquests, but journalists should avoid exacerbating distress and respect requests to desist. Special care for approaches that may harass those suffering grief or shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting suicide and self-harm (code clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting suicide or self-harm, journalists should be conscious of the risk of encouraging others and therefore care should be taken to avoid excessive detail of the methods used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance with media's right to report legal proceedings; see related clause on intrusion into grief/shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children (code clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children (anyone aged 17 and under) should be free to complete school without unnecessary intrusion and must not be approached or photographed at school without permission of school authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children under 18 must not be interviewed or photographed on issues involving their or another child's welfare without consent from someone with parental responsibility or similarly responsible adult. Children must not be paid for material about themselves (or their parents for material about them) unless clearly in the child's interest. Editors must not use a parent's fame/notoriety as sole justification for publishing details of a child's private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children in sexual offence cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not, even if legally free, identify children aged 17 or under who are victims or witnesses in cases involving sexual offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In press reports of sexual offences involving a child: the child must not be identified; subject to court order the adult may be identified; do not use the word 'incest' where it might identify a child victim; take care nothing implies the relationship between accused and child. Seek legal and senior editorial advice as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must identify themselves and obtain permission from a responsible executive before entering non-public areas of hospitals or similar institutions to pursue inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions on intruding into privacy are particularly relevant in hospitals; treat patients and privacy with special care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Relatives or friends of persons convicted or accused should not generally be identified without their consent unless genuinely relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay particular regard to naming victims, avoiding invasive/graphic detail or images compromising dignity; consider vulnerable position of children; generally avoid naming children arrested before youth court unless name already public or guardian consent obtained. Right to report court proceedings unaffected where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clandestine devices and subterfuge (code clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not seek to obtain or publish material acquired by hidden cameras, clandestine listening devices, intercepting private communications, unauthorised removal of documents/photos, or accessing digitally held information without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentation or subterfuge, including by agents/intermediaries, can be justified only in the public interest and only when material cannot be obtained by other means; such actions require senior editorial and legal discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victims of sexual assault (identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not identify victims of sexual assault or publish material likely to lead to identification unless there is adequate justification and publication is legally permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If identification is justified, permission from the relevant senior duty editor is required and legal advice should be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination and incitement to hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must avoid prejudicial or pejorative reference to protected characteristics and must avoid details of those characteristics unless genuinely relevant to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protected characteristics listed include race, colour, ethnicity, nationality, religion, age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability, physical or mental illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not use for personal profit financial information received in advance of general publication, nor pass such information to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose to editor/head of business any significant personal/close family financial interests in shares/securities written about; do not trade on securities you have covered recently or intend to cover; avoid conflicts and disclose interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have a moral obligation to protect confidential sources of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protecting sources is an ethical duty; consult senior duty editor when anonymity requested; follow technical/InfoSec guidance and training on source protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness payments in criminal trials
rubrics_metrics.description: No payment or offer of payment to a witness (or likely witness) should be made once proceedings are active as defined by Contempt of Court Act 1981.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibition lasts until suspect freed unconditionally or proceedings discontinued or verdict delivered. Where proceedings not yet active but likely, journalists must not make/offer payments; rare exceptions require senior duty editor and editorial legal discussion. Any payment made to a person later cited as witness must be disclosed to prosecution and defence and witness advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment to criminals
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment or offers for stories, pictures or information that exploit or glorify crime must not be made to convicted/confessed criminals or their associates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoking public interest to justify payment requires demonstration of good reason that the public interest would be served; payments must be discussed in advance with senior duty editor and director of editorial legal; if no public interest emerges material should not be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest (definition and tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of the public interest used by GNM (based on Ipso Editors’ Code) and procedural expectations for invoking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public interest includes detecting/exposing crime/serious impropriety; protecting public health/safety; protecting public from being misled; disclosing failure to comply with obligations; disclosing miscarriages of justice; raising/contributing to public debate on serious impropriety; disclosing concealment of the above. Consider whether material is already public and its contribution to debate. Journalists should discuss invoking public interest with senior editors/legal, must be able to demonstrate belief that publication would serve and be proportionate to public interest, and an exceptional public interest is needed to override normally paramount interests of children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and objectivity (guidance A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should take care to be accurate; significant errors must be corrected promptly; news reporters should strive for fairness and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant corrections should be handled through the readers' editor. Reporters should recognise how personal biases could affect reporting and work to be fair and objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous contributions (guidance B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should be published anonymously or pseudonymously only in exceptional circumstances where safety, privacy or livelihood would be compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider motive and alternatives; permission of relevant senior duty editor needed; established pseudonyms commissioned need not follow this; regular anonymous columns require editor-in-chief or equivalent approval. Where anonymity offered, be diligent in providing it and inform readers that identities have been obscured or withheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous quotations (guidance C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to attribute information to its source; anonymous quotations should generally be avoided though sometimes useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use indiscriminately. Anonymous pejorative quotes permitted only rarely and after senior duty editor consultation; otherwise paraphrase pejorative quotes. Bear in mind anonymous quotes can confer unfair advantage and reduce reader's ability to assess source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children (guidance D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special care for children (defined as 17 and under); they merit special protection as less aware of risks and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should consider withholding names/photos due to online longevity; do not photograph/interview without parental consent on welfare matters; exceptional cases require senior duty editor/legal; sometimes acceptable to interview without consent but without identifying details; special considerations for children commissioned to write; applies to journalists considering making their own children the subject of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital enhancement of images and multimedia (guidance E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Video, audio, images, montages and illustrations should generally not be digitally enhanced or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare exceptions must be approved in advance by the relevant senior duty editor and clearly labelled. See also picture desk guidance and section P on pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct quotations (guidance F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotations should not be changed to alter their context or meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer also to the Guardian style guide for quote handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors and amendment requests (guidance G)
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM’s policy is to correct significant errors as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All complaints, corrections and amendment requests should be brought to the readers' editor. Journalists must cooperate frankly, openly and promptly. Read daily correction columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative AI describes AI that creates text, images, video, audio or code; it can be used responsibly as part of journalism but raises issues around bias, ownership, plagiarism and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material created or adapted with GenAI is unreliable and tends to introduce unpredictable errors. Work under your byline must have been authored by you; journalists are accountable for their journalism. GenAI should enhance, not replace, journalists; active human oversight is essential. Any significant use must be explicitly approved by the relevant senior duty editor and clearly signalled to users in line with transparency guidelines and the Guardian’s Generative AI principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grief (guidance I)
rubrics_metrics.description: People should be treated with sensitivity during periods of personal grief and trauma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wait until death is formally confirmed and family notified before identifying deceased in most circumstances, unless impracticable (e.g., police need public identification). Avoid approaches that may harass grieving people; respect requests to desist; consider international readership and exercise sensitivity for distant events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance labels and distressing content (J)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphic or violent details should be included only when essential to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preface audio/video/photos likely to cause distress with warnings/explanations/labels when editorially justified. Labels are not generally necessary on articles where headlines and trails indicate subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewees (K)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat interviewees and subjects with respect, fairness and dignity; ensure they understand you are a journalist and that your questions are for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify on/off the record/background terms clearly if agreed. Give special consideration to victims of crime/tragedy, children and vulnerable people (including those with disabilities or memory-related conditions). See clauses on subterfuge and covert behaviour when arranging interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use language that reflects Guardian values and societal changes; adhere to the Guardian style guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care writing about sensitive issues and protected characteristics; add footnotes to support organisations where appropriate. Avoid using swearwords outside direct quotes unless essential; stronger swearwords in opinion pieces require greater care; avoid swearwords in headlines and never use asterisks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major incident reporting and unfolding events (M)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting major incidents (terrorism, natural disasters) remain objective, verify information before publication, and avoid speculation, stereotypes and sensationalist language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk to the relevant senior duty editor before publishing or linking to live footage or material by perpetrators. Consider safety of individuals caught up in events. Many code clauses (accuracy, privacy, harassment, grief, children, hospitals) are relevant; consult Ipso guidance and specialist reports where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental health (N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take particular care with stories about mental health; do not mention or speculate about a person’s mental health unless directly relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include helpline information where relevant (example contacts provided for UK, US, Australia). Refer to the Guardian style guide section on mental health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open court reporting and inquests (O)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting from open court and inquests is generally legally safe if fair and accurate, but invasive, insensitive or graphic details, or images compromising dignity, require careful consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must justify inclusion of such details; particularly graphic details should be published only after consulting the relevant senior duty editor and legal services where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures and video (P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care when using images or footage that may be invasive, insensitive or graphic and consider human dignity when selecting images to illustrate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid disrespectful images that could harm depicted individuals and others with similar issues. Government handout photographs should be used only if they have news value and must be clearly labelled. Consult the picture desk if in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must not represent others’ work as their own and must not reproduce other people’s material without attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are rare (e.g., unidentified source) and only with permission of the relevant senior duty editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy (guidance R) - photography and video; identifying details
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy is both an ethical consideration and a legally enforceable right; potential intrusions require prior consideration of public interest and senior duty editor authorisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with photography/filming where individuals reasonably expect privacy or are unaware pictures are being taken for publication; long-lens photography may be relevant when assessing intrusion. Avoid publishing identifying details (street names, house numbers) that enable intrusion on privacy or safety. Do not conduct 'fishing' expeditions; be able to demonstrate why an infringement of privacy is justified in the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the Omand principles (privacy assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use five Omand questions to assess proportionality before infringing privacy: sufficient cause; integrity of motive; proportionality of methods; proper authority; reasonable prospect of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should be able to demonstrate answers to these questions when intruding on privacy. Seek senior duty editor and legal guidance if in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: The right to reply (S)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every effort to contact the person or organisation who is the subject of a story before publication to put allegations to them and give them an opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assists accuracy and fairness and demonstrates consideration of the public interest. Account for complexity and time zones; the more serious the allegation, the greater the obligation to allow response. Editorial legal services can advise on best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources (T)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a source seeks anonymity or confidentiality, discuss the request with the relevant senior duty editor; protect confidential sources as a moral obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, identify other sources as specifically as possible. See also policy on anonymous contributions and confidential sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing - social media (U)
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM editorial code covers content published on social media as well as print and online; treat material from social media with the same legal, copyright and ethical considerations as any other source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarise with GNM social media guidelines before accessing, publishing or sharing material from social media or the wider internet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subterfuge and covert behaviour (V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should identify themselves as GNM employees (or freelancers on assignment) when gathering material; rare public interest exceptions for subterfuge require prior approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any material offered by third parties that involves surreptitious methods should be referred immediately to the managing editor and editorial legal. Policy applies to material obtained by hidden devices or by subterfuge of others, even if not published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide and self-harm (guidance W)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise particular care with stories about suicide and self-harm, bearing in mind the risk of encouraging others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid detailed methods; refer to substances/methods in general terms where possible; avoid speculation suggesting single/simple motives; avoid images that could act as 'triggers' (places where suicides occurred, scars); consider relatives' feelings and consult senior editors/legal as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification (X)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification is a core requirement for GNM journalism (listed in the code headings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify information before publication, particularly in breaking/unfolding events and when material originates from social media; seek corroboration and consult senior duty editor for live or unclear material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of hospitality, travel and gifts (professional behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: When hospitality, travel or accommodation is offered by an external interest (eg airline, hotel, sponsor), this must be made clear and disclosed in footnotes on relevant articles/content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of such offers is conditional on GNM being free to assign and report, or not report, any resulting story as it sees fit. Journalists should not be accompanied on free trips by partners/family unless exceptional and cleared; additional costs by companions should be paid by the journalist. Gifts other than perishable/low-value (<£50) should be returned or donated to charity; items supplied for reviews/photo shoots should be returned or stored/donated if impractical to return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freelance work and media appearances (professional behaviour K)
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time staff should not contribute to other publications or media outlets without prior authorisation from the managing editor; consult communications team before TV/media appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests to film inside GNM offices must be sent to media.enquiries@theguardian.com for approval. Follow approval processes; ensure appearances are appropriate and prepared.

rubrics_metrics.name: GNM connections (professional behaviour L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not use their positions to seek personal business or commercial advantages not afforded to the public generally and should not cite a Guardian connection to resolve consumer grievances or seek discounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use GNM email/social accounts for non-GNM matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers of financial assistance (professional behaviour M)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not act as intermediaries for donations or fundraising beyond putting people in contact if both parties willing; staff should not set up crowdfunders connected with Guardian articles or link to appeals without approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval by senior duty editor is required for linking to fundraising appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside interests and engagements (professional behaviour N)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists have a private life but outside interests must not conflict with work or compromise editorial integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active political involvement may create actual/perceived conflicts; generally staff should not hold political office. Discuss with editor-in-chief/managing editor before undertaking outside employment likely to conflict, giving evidence to court, representing material connected to GNM publications, chairing/speaking at public events in capacity as GNM journalist. Approved public speaking within work hours should not be paid; travel/expenses may be accepted. Declare potential conflicts on biographies and consult managing editor when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments for stories (professional behaviour O)
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM does not pay sources or interviewees financially or via gifts/inducements except rare exceptions approved by the senior duty editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should not engage paid services of external non-journalistic agents or assistants without prior knowledge/approval of senior duty editor. Tip fees may be paid to bona fide freelance journalists on occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships (professional behaviour P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not generally commission, write about, photograph, film or make editorial decisions about individuals with whom they have close personal or financial relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether relationships with public figures or journalists create conflicts of interest and discuss with managing editor. Declare relevant relationships where they could affect professional duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct (professional behaviour Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat people with respect and professionalism on social media; anything posted privately can be shared publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarise with GNM social media guidelines and safety documents; think before posting and use common sense to avoid reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source care and protection (professional behaviour R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists working regularly with sources must understand practicalities and limitations of source protection and be realistic about technological and legal limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not promise outcomes beyond GNM's control. Attend InfoSec/legal training on source protection, ensure devices meet GNM encryption standards, use secure methods (eg Secure Drop), consider in-person or postal delivery when appropriate. Consult InfoSec and editorial legal where needed. Further resources provided (Protecting Sources and Whistleblowers in a Digital Age).
